This is a siege of Carthage that lasted many years in the third Punic War. The Romans, if they don’t like you, will come and kill everyone of you. That’s what they did to Carthage. During this war, a Greek named Palibius was a hostage of Rome and became the official historian of the Roman Empire. So he invented the Battle of Cannae to justify the burning of Carthage because the Romans asked, “Why did we kill the Carthaginians?” Because that’s what they do, man. But Palibius understood that if Rome is going to be an empire, it needs people on its side and must explain its actions. Thus, to justify the Roman Empire, Palibius created the entire history of the Punic War, which didn’t really happen.

Rome felt threatened by Hannibal, so they saw Carthage as a threat and had to destroy it for it to make sense. Palibus essentially made the entire history of Rome. Remember, if you’re a military power, you don’t write history because you can’t reflect or produce deep culture. Romans won battles and got Greeks to write their history to justify their actions. So all Roman history is complete nonsense.

After destroying Carthage, Rome became the undisputed leader of the Mediterranean but continued fighting wars overseas for no particular reason. The only way Rome could generate wealth was by conquering other people. Nobles wanted to fight these wars to capture slaves, who worked their estates. Slaves were the main resource being fought over at this time.

To fight these wars, peasants were conscripted into the military. Once away from their land, they needed to feed families and borrowed money with land as collateral. Over time, they couldn’t pay back interest, defaulted on loans, and lost their land. Then, landowners seized it and used conquered slaves to work it. Peasants had no choice but to go to Rome for work; the state provided food called a grain do. Nobles bribed peasants to vote for more wars, promising them booty.

The Roman war machine created slavery, debt, corruption, and inequality. Wealth became more consolidated in fewer hands, causing conflict between upper and lower nobility. Optimates were the upper class who believed they deserved wealth because of their superiority. Populares were lower class like Julius Caesar, who promised peasants opportunities to redistribute rich people’s wealth.

This conflict arose after Carthage’s destruction and lasted until the end of the Roman Empire. Even as an empire, Rome’s aggressive military energy translated into civil war.
